transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-05-14 15:00 PDT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Lin (Redwood AE), Carlos Gutierrez (Redwood SE), Priya Sharma (Aurora Infra), Liam O'Connor (Aurora Security), Noah Kim (Aurora Cloud)

[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya at Redwood Inference, AE on the account, and with me is Carlos, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Priya: Hey Maya, doing well. Thanks for coordinating. We'll try to keep this pretty focused — we're trying to validate networking patterns for a Private deployment.
[00:13] Liam: Hi, yes this is Liam, I'll jump in mostly on security questions.
[00:16] Noah: Noah here — cloud infra questions.
[00:18] Carlos: Great. Quick agenda — we want to understand your current AWS footprint, whether you need Transit Gateway or peering, DNS and PrivateLink needs, control plane connectivity, and any region/residency constraints. Does that match what you want to cover?
[00:28] Priya: Yep, that's exactly it. We run primarily in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. For health data we need eu residency for EU customers. For the pilot we'll use us-east-1 only, but long term multi-region is a requirement.
[00:40] Maya: Understood. Can you describe your VPC setup and whether you have a central TGW (Transit Gateway) or are you using pairwise peering?
[00:48] Priya: We have a central Transit Gateway in our prod AWS account that's attached to multiple account VPCs via AWS Resource Access Manager. For the trial we can create a dedicated VPC in our infra account or use a shared-services VPC, depends on what you recommend.
[01:00] Carlos: For Redwood Private deployments we support a few patterns. You can do VPC peering if it's single account/limited scale, Transit Gateway for multi-account scale and for cross-region we recommend Transit Gateway + TGW peering or using Transit Gateway inter-region attachments. We also support Direct Connect / ExpressRoute for private connectivity if you have on-prem.
[01:20] Noah: If we go Transit Gateway, do you create attachments from the Redwood-managed VPC or do we host the Redwood VPC in our account?
[01:27] Carlos: Both are supported. Typical enterprise pattern is Redwood deploys data plane into your AWS account as a set of CloudFormation/Terraform modules — that gives you full control over subnets, SGs, and NAT. Alternatively, for a managed-hosted private model, Redwood can host the data plane in a customer-dedicated account and peer/attach it to your TGW. Each has tradeoffs around auditability and support.
[01:48] Liam: Auditability matters. For healthcare data we want customer-owned VPCs and KMS keys for encryption at rest. Is that possible?
[01:55] Maya: Yes, customer-managed KMS is supported in Private deployments. We can integrate with your KMS keys (we'll need to provide the appropriate cross-account IAM roles) and you keep control of keys and rotation. We'll also emit audit logs to your CloudWatch/CloudTrail.
[02:09] Priya: Good. About Private endpoints — do you require internet egress to the Redwood control plane for updates/metrics, or can everything be fully private?
[02:18] Carlos: There are two models: 1) Private control plane: Redwood control plane can be deployed into your control VPC / private network — that requires a private connectivity arrangement to Redwood's control plane or a self-hosted control plane. 2) Semi-private: data plane fully private in your VPC, but data plane needs to reach Redwood control endpoints for telemetry, billing, and model catalog sync. For semi-private we provide a minimal egress footprint — usually TLS over 443 to a small set of FQDNs; we can also do AWS PrivateLink endpoints for control plane access if you prefer to avoid internet egress.
[02:48] Noah: If we need to avoid internet egress entirely, PrivateLink is the pattern? We have strict egress policies for the PHI scope.
[02:55] Carlos: PrivateLink is the recommended approach to avoid public internet. Redwood can publish a service endpoint in our account and you create an interface endpoint in yours. That supports control plane traffic over a private ENI — DNS routing and split-horizon DNS need to be configured so your calls resolve to the interface endpoint.
[03:11] Priya: Are there any ports besides 443? Do we need outbound to any IP ranges?
[03:16] Carlos: For default operation, it's TCP 443 outbound to our control-plane FQDNs. If you choose PrivateLink, then it's internal to AWS and just normal HTTPS to the interface endpoint. For optional telemetry or metrics collectors we can also publish a list of small CIDR blocks if you run tighter egress controls. We'll supply a minimal allowlist.
[03:34] Liam: KMS cross-account role flow — what are the exact permissions we need to grant? Anything that would trip our security review?
[03:41] Maya: We'll provide a Security SRD that lists the exact IAM policies and the least-privilege KMS grants. Typically Redwood needs kms:Decrypt for model artifacts in S3 (if you choose customer key) and kms:GenerateDataKey for runtime. We'll outline key policies that allow the Redwood service principal or an assumed role to use the key.
[03:58] Priya: About CIDR overlap — our org commonly uses 10.0.0.0/8 ranges. We have had problems with peering and overlapping blocks when vendors try to peer. How do you handle overlap?
[04:08] Carlos: Overlapping CIDR is a common blocker. Options: 1) Deploy Redwood data plane into a unique CIDR you carve out in your tenancy; 2) Use NAT/egress patterns where outbound traffic is SNATed to a non-overlapping egress IP; 3) Use PrivateLink since it doesn't require route table propagation or unique VPC CIDR. For Transit Gateway attachments, you must ensure non-overlapping routes between attachments.
[04:31] Noah: For PrivateLink, what's the DNS setup? We do split-horizon with Route53 private hosted zones.
[04:36] Carlos: We recommend using Route53 private hosted zones or a DNS forwarder. When you create the interface endpoint, the default AWS DNS will return the endpoint ENI IPs. If you use custom names, you can create A/CNAME records in your private zone pointing to the interface endpoint. We'll give sample Route53 configs.
[04:53] Liam: Logging — can audit logs go to our CloudTrail? Also retention policies?
[04:58] Maya: Yes, we can route control plane audit logs to your account via CloudWatch/CloudTrail ingestion. For data plane request logs, we can emit structured logs to your S3 or CloudWatch. Retention is configurable on your side; Redwood will provide retention recommendations for compliance.
[05:13] Priya: Any special requirements for subnets — public vs private? We generally lock down public subnets.
[05:19] Carlos: For nodes that need outbound internet egress (if you choose that pattern) they'll be in private subnets with NAT gateway. For interface endpoints and control-plane attached components, private subnets with ENIs are typical. We'll provide recommended AZ spread, subnet sizing for GPU nodes, and example security group rules.
[05:36] Noah: GPU nodes — do you require specific instance types and are there any IP-level requirements for node-to-node communication?
[05:42] Carlos: We recommend A10/A100 or T4s depending on model and quantization. Node-to-node is over private networking inside the VPC — we need intra-cluster connectivity on certain ports (we'll list them). Usually security groups allow all traffic within the cluster SG. We can document the exact port ranges; it's mostly ephemeral and RPC ports plus control-plane health checks.
[06:00] Priya: On region constraints: for EU residency we need the model artifacts and logs to remain in eu-west-1. Does Redwood support pinning data plane by region?
[06:07] Maya: Yes, you can pin the data plane to a region. For multi-region we deploy separate data planes in each region; control plane interactions can be regionalized or routed through a regional control plane instance depending on the architecture. We'll include an options doc on multi-region deployments and cross-region replication constraints.
[06:26] Liam: What about compliance docs — SOC2, penetration test, whitepapers?
[06:30] Maya: We'll send our security package: SOC 2 Type II summary, pen-test results redacted, privacy and data-processing agreement, and our Private Deployment security checklist.
[06:38] Priya: That would be helpful. Also, are there any managed network components you expect us to operate (bastion, jump hosts) for support?
[06:44] Carlos: We sometimes ask for a jump host or session manager access for remote debugging, but it's optional. Preferred pattern: we use SSM session-manager with cross-account role and no bastion. We'll detail the least-privilege roles needed.
[06:56] Noah: Regarding cost — if we host data plane in our account, are there expected infra costs we should budget? GPU reservations etc?
[07:03] Maya: Yes if you bring your own infra you'll pay for the EC2/GPU and networking. Redwood charges for the Private deployment software license and optionally for managed ops. For Dedicated/reserved capacity we can provide a cost estimate. We'll follow up with a ballpark.
[07:17] Priya: We plan a 6-week pilot starting late June. Minimal scope: a single VPC in us-east-1, sample healthcare prompt workload, end-to-end redaction controls. What do you need to get started?
[07:27] Maya: For the pilot we need your VPC diagram & CIDRs, desired AZs/subnets, preferred deployment model (data plane in your account vs Redwood-managed), a short security point-of-contact, and access for our SE to perform a network deep-dive. Once we have that we'll produce a pilot runbook and an estimated infra bill.
[07:44] Priya: We'll get that together.
[07:47] [~mid call interruption noise]
[07:52] Liam: Quick question — certificate management. Do we need to supply certs for PrivateLink or does Redwood manage certificates for internal endpoints?
[07:59] Carlos: For PrivateLink the interface endpoint uses AWS-managed certificates for the TLS handshake to the service DNS name. If you need mTLS between your services and the data plane, we support mutual TLS using customer certs. We'll outline both flows.
[08:14] Maya: Alright I'll recap and propose next steps — share network checklist and security pack by Friday, and schedule a 60-minute network deep-dive with your networking team for next week.
[08:23] Priya: Works for us. Liam and Noah will attend the deep-dive as well.
[08:26] Carlos: One more thing — overlapping CIDR workaround example: we'll include a Terraform snippet that shows deploying the data plane into a non-overlapping /20 and configuring NAT to SNAT egress to a static Elastic IP you own, that often helps with third-party integrations that expect known egress IPs.
[08:42] Priya: That's great.
[08:44] Maya: Any final questions?
[08:46] Liam: Nothing else right now, just want to make sure the security docs come through.
[08:49] Priya: No more from infra.
[08:51] Maya: Perfect. We'll follow up via email and update the CRM. Thanks everyone.
[08:56] Priya: Thanks, bye.
[08:58] Noah: Bye.
